notes.text: Your e-pawn stakes a claim in the center, controlling d5 and f5.
notes.original: White starts the game trying to take control of the center.

notes.text: Black won't give up the center without a fight, so the e5 pawn meets yours.
notes.original: Black of course doesn't want to give up the center without a fight, so they play e5.

notes.text: Your knight develops and attacks the e5 pawn.
notes.original: White retaliates to this with Nf6, threatening the e5 pawn.

notes.text: Black's knight defends the e5 pawn.
notes.original: Black defends the e5 pawn with the move Nc6. This can lead to many different openings and positions, but white chooses to challenge and put pressure on the c6 knight with the move Bb5.

notes.text: Your bishop pressures the c6 knight; this is the start of the Ruy Lopez.
notes.original: This is now the starting position of the Ruy Lopez. From this point on, the opening branches out to 3 different variations. This could lead to the Closed/Open Ruy Lopez, the Berlin Defense, and the Exchange Variations. Black has multiple options from this point, but the most common move a6, challenging the light squared bishop.

notes.text: Black's a-pawn challenges your bishop; you can take on c6 or retreat to a4.
notes.original: White can do one of two things here. They can either exchange the bishop for the knight which leads to exchange variation or they can retreat to a4.

notes.text: The Berlin Defense is one of Black's best answers to the Ruy Lopez, made famous by Kramnik against Kasparov.
notes.original: This move leads to the variation known as the Berlin Defense. This variation provides really good chances for black and is one of black's best responses to the Ruy Lopez. This variation was popularized after Vladmir Kramnik used it in his championship game against Garry Kasparov and he went on to win the game. Since then, the position has been heavily analyzed and is a very common opening nowadays. The theory must be known by any Ruy Lopez player.

notes.text: Retreating to a4 is the most common choice and keeps the pressure on the c6 knight.
notes.original: This is the most common move after a6, the idea is to maintain the pressure the knight on c6.

notes.text: The Exchange Variation: you take the knight, which defends the center, and double Black's pawns at once.
notes.original: This is considered to be the exchange variation of the Ruy Lopez. The idea here is to remove a defender of the center and to double black's pawns straight away rather than retreat the bishop.

notes.text: The Exchange Variation removes a defender of the center and doubles Black's pawns; you rely on your kingside majority.
notes.original: This known as the exchange variation of the Ruy Lopez. The point here is to remove a defender of the center and to double black's pawns immediately. White will rely on his pawn majority on the king-side. Black has to capture with the d-pawn.

notes.text: Black develops the knight and pressures your e4 pawn.
notes.original: Simply a developing move, also putting pressure on the center and on the e4 pawn.

notes.text: You castle to get your king out of the center; Re1 will then support the e-pawn.
notes.original: White wants to get their king out of the center quickly and also support the e-pawn with the move Re1. Black's main move here is Be7, but they doesn't have to play this. Black can play in a much more aggresive fashion if they choose to do so.

notes.text: Your d3 simply defends the e-pawn and sidesteps all the main theory.
notes.original: If white wants to try and throw off their opponent, they can play the move d3. This move simply defends the e-pawn but also avoids all theoretical openings.

notes.text: Black develops the bishop to prepare castling; this begins the Closed Ruy Lopez.
notes.original: Another developing move, trying to get their king out of the center. This is the start of the Closed Ruy Lopez.

notes.text: This is the Closed Ruy Lopez: Black develops instead of taking e4, and the position is fairly equal.
notes.original: This is the starting position of the Closed Ruy Lopez. Black chooses not to take the pawn on e4 and instead they go for development. The Closed Ruy Lopez is played even at the highest levels and it leads to multiple different variations. The Closed Ruy Lopez provides better chances than the Open Ruy Lopez and is a fairly equal position. The rest of the line goes as follows.

notes.text: The Open Ruy Lopez gives Black chances, but you can attack sooner while Black's king sits in the center.
notes.original: This is known as the Open Ruy Lopez. This gives more attacking chances for black but white can attack much sooner because black's king is still in the center.

notes.text: Black grabs your e4 pawn, a slightly risky choice; answer by striking in the center yourself.
notes.original: This is called the Open Ruy Lopez. Rather than playing a closed position, black chooses to strike in the center immediately by taking the pawn on e4. This opening is considered to be better for white, but it still provides chances for either side. This may be considered to be a little risky because black in underdeveloped and the e-file could be potentially opened for white's rook. Black still will have enough resources to support the knight on e4 positionally. White takes advantage of this opening by striking in the center as well.

notes.text: Your rook takes the e-file and protects the e4 pawn, reaching the Closed Ruy Lopez.
notes.original: White wants to control the e-file and to protect their pawn on e4 as well. After this move, we have reached the starting position of the Closed Ruy Lopez.

notes.text: Your rook protects the e4 pawn and becomes active.
notes.original: Protecting the pawn on e4 and activating the rook.

notes.text: Black attacks your active bishop on a4 with the b-pawn.
notes.original: Just before castling, black again tries to attack white's most active piece.

notes.text: Black's pawn attacks your bishop and forces it to retreat.
notes.original: Attacking the bishop and forcing the bishop to retreat.

notes.text: Your bishop retreats to b3 and eyes the f7 pawn; it usually ends up on c2.
notes.original: White's only move is to move the bishop to b3, putting pressure on the f-pawn. However in most variations, white's bishop will end up on c2.

notes.text: Your bishop has to retreat.
notes.original: White needs to retreat the bishop.

notes.text: Black finally castles and is ready to start an attack.
notes.original: Black finally gets their king of the center and is ready to start an attack.

notes.text: Black simply gets the king out of the center.
notes.original: Simply getting the king out of the center.

notes.text: This prepares d4; Black can go for the Marshall Attack with d5 or play d6.
notes.original: This move is in preparation for the move d4. From this point this can branch out to the Marshall Attack with the move d5 or other variations with the move d6. This position is seen commonly in top level games.

notes.text: Your c3 prepares to strike in the center with d4.
notes.original: Preparing to attack in the center with the move d4.

notes.text: This stops the Marshall Attack, but you give up your opening edge; the games get complex and fun.
notes.original: This is another move that white can play that prevents the Marshall Attack, however this one of the more complex lines because white gives up all of the opening advantage that they had. However, this move produces very fun games.

notes.text: The Anti-Marshall: your a-pawn hits b5, so Black must deal with it, and you avoid the heavily analysed Marshall.
notes.original: As you can see, this variation is literally called the Anti-Marshall. This move prevents the move d4 to occur because black needs to do something about their b5 pawn. Reasons why white may want to do this is because they may be trying to go for a win and/or because the Marshall Attack has been so heavily analyzed that it'll most likely end up being a draw.

notes.text: Your h-pawn takes g4 away, so Black's bishop can never come there, which also stops the Marshall.
notes.original: This move can also prevent the Marshall Attack because it prevents the bishop from ever coming to g4.

notes.text: Black supports the e5 pawn and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop.
notes.original: Black tries to support the e-pawn with the move d6. This move also opens up the diagonal for their light-squared bishop which can possibly pin the knight to the queen.

notes.text: Black's d6 supports the e5 pawn and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop.
notes.original: Supporting the pawn on e5 and opening up the diagonal for the light-squared bishop.

notes.text: The Marshall Attack: Black strikes at your e4 pawn at once, the most aggressive weapon against the Ruy Lopez.
notes.original: This variation is the known as the Marshall Attack. This move strikes in the center immediately and it's the most aggressive weapon against the Ruy Lopez. A sample goes as follows, a more in-depth review will be covered in a separate chapter.

notes.text: This is the Marshall Attack, a popular, aggressive line that gives Black fighting chances.
notes.original: This known as the Marshall Attack. The Marshall Attack is one of the most popular and most interesting lines in the Ruy Lopez. This is a very dangerous and aggresive opening which gives black fighting chances.

notes.text: Your h-pawn stops Black's bishop from reaching g4.
notes.original: White doesn't allow the bishop to get to g4. After this point, white is allowing black to choose how they want to continue the game. Black has multiple moves in this position, all leading towards different variations. White's main plan is to the d4 pawn and get the undeveloped knight to the g3. Black has a few ideas as well, including moving the f-knight to d7 in order to push the f-pawn to f5. Another idea is to move the c-knight to a5 in order to push the c-pawn to c5.

notes.text: Your plan: push d4, then bring the b1 knight around to g3.
notes.original: White doesn't allow the bishop to get to g4. After this point, white is allowing black to choose how they want to continue the game. Black has multiple moves in this position, all leading towards different variations. White's main plan is to the d4 pawn and get the undeveloped knight to the g3. Black has a few ideas as well, including moving the f-knight to d7 in order to push the f-pawn to f5. Another idea is to move the c-knight to a5 in order to push the c-pawn to c5.

notes.text: Here the Closed Ruy Lopez splits into many variations, and the position is equal.
notes.original: This the part of the main line where the Closed Ruy Lopez splits into many different variations. Black can play the Breyer Variation, the Chigorin Variation, and more. White still needs to develop their pieces on the queen-side and black needs to get their pieces in a better position to attack. The position is considered to be equal for both sides.

notes.text: This is the Breyer: Black reroutes the knight to d7, where it defends e5.
notes.original: This is referred to as the Breyer variation of the Ruy Lopez. The point is to re-maneuver black's knight to d7 and to push the c and d pawns in the future. Putting the knight on d7 also defends the e5 pawn. The lines for this variation will be covered in a separate chapter as well.

notes.text: In the solid Breyer, Black's knight retreats to b8 so it can reroute to d7.
notes.original: This position is known as the Breyer variation of the Ruy Lopez. The variation got its name from Gyula "Julius" Breyer who was a Hungarian chess prodigy. He contributed to the theory of this opening and that's why this variation was named after him. This is a very solid way to fight against the Ruy Lopez for black. This move may seem strange at first but it's actually a very sensical option. The knight wants to re-maneuver to d7 where it can support e5 and c5 and black wants to push the c-pawn. Lastly, black also wants to put the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal.

notes.text: In the Chigorin, Black's knight attacks your bishop on b3 and prepares c5.
notes.original: This move leads to the Chigorin variation of the Ruy Lopez. The point here is to attack the Bishop on b3 and to play c5.

notes.text: The Chigorin: Black's knight chases your bishop, then c5 and a return to c6 build a stronger center.
notes.original: I'm going to go further in-depth with the Closed Ruy Lopez variations because they are much more commonly played rather than the Open Ruy Lopez variations. 9. Na5 is known as the Chigorin Variation of the Closed Ruy Lopez. This is one of the most aggressive variations for black. The idea is to chase the bishop away and to get a stronger center by playing c5 and retreating the knight back to c6.

notes.text: You keep your bishop by moving it out of danger instead of trading it.
notes.original: White doesn't want to trade the bishop, so they get it out of danger.

notes.text: You retreat the bishop to c2 so it isn't traded for Black's misplaced knight on a5.
notes.original: White does not want trade his most powerful piece for the misplaced knight so white retreats it to another active diagonal.

notes.text: Black's c5 adds pressure on the center and frees c6 for the knight to return.
notes.original: The idea of c5 is to not only put more pressure on the center, but to also put their knight on more useful square, c6. The lines for this variation will be covered on separate chapter.

notes.text: Black pushes c5 so the a5 knight can return to c6 without blocking the pawn.
notes.original: Black sticks to their plan and pushes c5 so that the knight may retreat without blocking in the pawn.

notes.text: Black can strike with d5 instead of c5, putting tension on your e4 pawn.
notes.original: Black doesn't have to play c5, instead they can play a much more aggressive sideline, d5. This move immediately creates tension in the center.

notes.text: Black gets a swift attack as compensation: your pieces are undeveloped and your bishop on b3 is nearly useless.
notes.original: This is the starting position of the of the Marshall Attack. The compensation for black is that white has 4 undeveloped pieces and their bishop on b3 is essentially useless in these lines. What black gets is a swift attack. The story of this opening goes as this. Frank Marshall prepared this attack for 10 years against Jose Raul Capablanca, one of the greatest chess players of all time. When he got to play it, he lost it because he played a line which nowadays, it's considered inaccurate.

notes.text: c6 is Black's best: it guards the knight on d5 against your rook and bishop.
notes.original: This is the best way for black to continue the Marshall attack. This allows for black to keep the light-squared bishop in the attack against white and it also protects black from white's double attack on the knight.

notes.text: This is the original Marshall Attack, but it is inferior because the knight move blocks in the bishop.
notes.original: This is known as the Original Marshall Attack which Frank Marshall played against Jose Raul Capablanca. However, it's best to play a6 rather than to move the knight away. It's inferior because it blocks in the bishop.

notes.text: This is not the best move: the bishop is less useful on b7 than on c8.
notes.original: This move is not considered to be the best move because once again, the bishop isn't really as useful as it was in c8, which is why a6 is the best move.

notes.text: d4 is best: it supports your rook on e5 and opens the way to develop your pieces.
notes.original: d4 is the best move here as white has been preparing to play this move the entire game. This move supports the rook and also opens up the opportunity for white to develop the rest of their pieces later on.

notes.text: Black's bishop attacks your overextended rook and prepares a dangerous attack on your king.
notes.original: Black should now attack the overextended rook and prepare to launch a very dangerous attack against the king if white is not careful.

notes.text: Putting the rook back on e1 is the best thing you can do.
notes.original: The best thing for white to do is to put the rook back on e1.

notes.text: Black's queen and bishop bear down on h2; g3 is your only move that holds.
notes.original: The only move for black that compensates for giving up the pawn is Qh4, keeping the attack on white going. As you can see, Black has 3 very powerful pieces all trying to attack on the king-side meanwhile white has three undeveloped pieces that are currently doing nothing. The ONLY move after Qh4 is g3. Any other move is winning for black.

notes.text: g3 is the only move that doesn't lose: it hits the queen and shuts the bishop's diagonal.
notes.original: White plays the only move in this position that doesn't lose for white.

notes.text: Beginners often play h3 to stop Qxh3, but this loses to the bishop sacrifice.
notes.original: A mistake that a lot of beginner Ruy Lopez players will make is that they will play h3, stopping Qxh3. However, this is now losing for white because black can just sacrifice the bishop in this position and it is actually the only move that provides black an advantage here.

notes.text: Black keeps the queen in the attack and eyes g2; you have four common ways to defend.
notes.original: Again, if black does not want white to gain an advantage, they should not retreat the queen and instead, keep the queen in the attack. Now black's plan is to try and checkmate white on g2. There are a four main ways that white can defend here that are commonly played.

notes.text: In the Arkhangelsk, Black builds a lot of pressure on your e4 pawn.
notes.original: This is known as the the Arkhangelsk (Archangel) variation of the Ruy Lopez. Black has created a lot of pressure in the center, especially the e4 pawn. The lines for this variation will be covered in a separate variation.

notes.text: This is the Arkhangelsk: Black risks the king in the centre for rapid development and an active bishop.
notes.original: This version of the Ruy Lopez is known as the Arkhangelsk variation. This is one of the most aggressive defenses that black could choose against the Ruy Lopez. This version is named after the city that the Russian Grandmasters devised the defense. The idea of the this variation is that it neglects the king's safety and leaves it in the center but, black gets rapid development as compensation. As you can see, black has a very active bishop aiming towards the king-side.

notes.text: You hold a pawn majority on the kingside and plan to develop rapidly.
notes.original: At this point, white is counting on his pawn majority on the kingside and plans to develop rapidly. The lines for the exchange variation will be covered in a separate chapter.

notes.text: Black has to retake with the d-pawn.
notes.original: Black of course has to take back the bishop with the d-pawn.

notes.text: Black must defend the e5 pawn, most commonly with f6.
notes.original: Black has to defend the e5 pawn. They can do this in multiple ways but the most common way to defend the pawn is f6.

notes.text: Instead of castling, this heads for a quick queen trade, where the author thinks Black is better.
notes.original: This is an alternative to castling straight away. Black will continue to play f6 but the main line leads to a quick queen trade and in my opinion, black is better.

notes.text: Another Exchange Variation: you challenge the center at once and plan an early queen trade.
notes.original: This is another variation of the exchange variation that white can play. White immediately challenges the center and plans to trade the queens early on.

notes.text: Don't take the e5 pawn: Black's queen move wins it back, so just develop normally.
notes.original: If white should take this pawn, play Qd4, winning back the pawn or possibly the knight should your opponent blunder. This is a very common opening trap for black. Do not take the pawn as white, just play normally.

notes.text: Grabbing the e5 pawn is dubious: Black's queen fork wins the pawn right back.
notes.original: This is a very common opening trap in the exchange variation of the Ruy Lopez. White may think that since the e4 pawn is undefended, they can take it but they this is a dubious move. Reason being is that black can immediately win the pawn back with the move Qd4.

notes.text: The queen forks your knight and the e4 pawn; Black regains the pawn or wins the knight if you slip.
notes.original: The queen forks the knight and the pawn, black will either gain back the pawn or capture the knight if white blunders.

notes.text: Retreating the knight to f3 is your only move, and it hits the queen.
notes.original: This is white's only move.

notes.text: Black's queen takes back the pawn with check.
notes.original: Take back the pawn as so.

notes.text: Black regains the pawn with check, and you must trade queens or end up much worse.
notes.original: Black regains the pawn and White is forced to trade queens or white will be at a severe disadvantage.

notes.text: Castling heads for the Berlin endgame; a sample line shows how it unfolds.
notes.original: This leads to the Berlin endgame. A sample line goes as follows, and in-depth review of the Berlin Defense will be covered in a separate chapter.

notes.text: The main alternative to the Berlin: d3 supports your e4 pawn, so Black can't capture it.
notes.original: This is the main alternative to the Berlin Endgame. This move solidifies the e4 pawn. It doesn't allow black to capture.

notes.text: Your d4 pawn keeps fighting for the center while Black's king is still on e8.
notes.original: This when the Berlin Endgame would occur, white is still battling for the center, meanwhile trying to exploit the fact that black's king is still on e8 and undefended.

notes.text: You lead in development and Black can't castle, but your e5 pawn is weak. Good moves: Rd1+, h3, Nc3.
notes.original: This one of the most theoretical openings in all of chess. White has castled and has a clear lead in development., but the e pawn is a weakness right now. As for black, he has reduced most of the tension, but black still needs to develop and he has forfeited castling rights. What black wants to do is get some initiative with his light-squared bishop and develop as soon as possible. White has 3 good moves, (in order of popularity) Rd1+, h3, & Nc3.

notes.text: Your d4 challenges the center, hitting c5 and e5, the move you have prepared all along.
notes.original: White doesn't allow for the knight to get back to c6 and plays d4 right away. The move d4 challenges the center and is basically the move that white has been preparing to play all along.

notes.text: Black's queen develops to c7 and guards the c5 and d6 pawns.
notes.original: Queen is developed in order to protect the c-pawn and the d-pawn

notes.text: Black can transpose into the Keres Defense, which is covered in another chapter.
notes.original: Black can choose to transpose into the Keres Defense which will be covered in another chapter.

notes.text: Black can take the pawn at once instead of playing queen c7 first, then develop the bishop.
notes.original: Black can take the pawn straight away rather than playing Qc7 first. Then they will develop their bishop.

notes.text: Black can play the Borisenko variation, putting the knight on c6 straight away.
notes.original: Black can play the Borisenko variation where they choose to put the knight on c6 straight away.

notes.text: Black can also develop the bishop to b7 straight away instead of playing queen c7.
notes.original: Black can also put the bishop on b7 straight away instead of playing Qc7.

notes.text: Reroute the knight to f5 via f1 and g3, develop the bishop to e3, and put a rook on c1.
notes.original: This is the main line of the Chigorin defense. The idea here for white is to re-maneuver their knight to f1, g3, and f5 which is a very common idea in the Closed Ruy Lopez. White will also get the bishop on e3 where it's on a much more active diagonal. Another idea is to get white's a-rook on c1 and attack the c-file. Black's ideas are to get their knight back to c6, get their bishop to f8 after the rook has moved to e8, and to get their bishop on b7 or d7 which are much more active diagonal. Black will also get their a-rook to c8 to challenge the c-file as well.

notes.text: Black takes the d4 pawn, challenging your center.
notes.original: Black takes the pawn, challenging the center.

notes.text: You simply recapture the pawn on d4.
notes.original: White simply recaptures.

notes.text: Black's knight finally returns to c6, following its original plan.
notes.original: Black continues to stick with his initial plan which was to get the knight back on c6.

notes.text: Your knight steps to b3, but your dark-squared bishop still needs developing.
notes.original: This move is defending the e4 square and white still needs to develop the dark-squared bishop.

notes.text: Black's a-pawn heads for a4 to kick your knight off b3.
notes.original: Black is going to attempt to kick out the knight from the b3 square.

notes.text: You develop the dark-squared bishop just in time, before the knight gets kicked out.
notes.original: White finally develops their dark-squared bishop just in time before the knight gets kicked out.

notes.text: Black's a-pawn gains queenside space and hits your knight on b3.
notes.original: Simply expanding on the queen-side and kicking out the knight.

notes.text: Your knight retreats to d2, where it supports the e4 pawn again.
notes.original: The knight needs to move and is supporting the e4 pawn once again.

notes.text: Black develops the bishop to d7; b7 would be less useful with the knight staying on c6.
notes.original: Developing the light-squared bishop, putting the bishop on b7 is fine but it's not useful since the knight is most likely going to stay on c6, guarding the center.

notes.text: Your rook goes to c1 to support the c-file; both sides are regrouping their pieces.
notes.original: White sticks to their plan, trying to support the c-file with the rook. Both sides have plans to remaneuver their pieces to much more useful positions.

notes.text: Black's queen takes a more active diagonal on b7 and avoids any discovered attack.
notes.original: Simply putting the queen on a more active diagonal and protecting the c-pawn. Also wants to prevent any kind of discovered attack.

notes.text: Your queen moves to e2, a more useful square.
notes.original: Simply moving the queen to a much more useful position.

notes.text: Black's rook goes to e8, reinforcing the e-file and the center.
notes.original: Reinforcing the e-file and the center.

notes.text: Your bishop leaves c2, opening the file for your rook and hitting the b5 pawn.
notes.original: Opening up the file for the rook and putting pressure on the b-pawn.

notes.text: Black's rook joins the b-file behind the queen, adding a defender for the b5 pawn.
notes.original: Reinforcing the b-file and adding an additional defender for the b-pawn.

notes.text: Your e5 pawn creates central tension and hits the f6 knight.
notes.original: Creating tension in the center and putting pressure on the f6 knight.

notes.text: Black takes back on e5 and invites a knight trade, so the d-pawn can support the center again.
notes.original: Recapturing the pawn and preparing to exchange the knights in the center of the board so that the d-pawn will once again reinforce the center for black.

notes.text: You simply trade knights on e5.
notes.original: Simply a piece exchange.

notes.text: Black keeps reinforcing the center; this main line goes on for a long time without branching.
notes.original: Sticking to the plan of reinforcing the center. The theory continues to go on for a while as the game doesn't branch for the while. Keep in mind, not every game goes this way but this is still considered to be the main line.

notes.text: Your bishop offers a trade of dark-squared bishops.
notes.original: Offering a exchange of dark-squared bishops

notes.text: Black's bishop adds pressure on your e4 pawn.
notes.original: Black puts additional pressure on the e4 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight returns to f3, a much more useful square.
notes.original: Re-maneuvering the knight to a much more useful square.

notes.text: Black's knight and bishop both hit your c5 bishop, threatening to win a piece.
notes.original: Black threatens to win a piece by capturing the bishop.

notes.text: You finally start the exchange by taking the e7 bishop.
notes.original: White finally initiates the exchange.

notes.text: Black recaptures the bishop with the rook.
notes.original: Black recaptures the bishop.

notes.text: Your rook supports the d3 bishop and helps stop a queenside pawn break.
notes.original: Reinforces the light-squared bishop and also tries to prevent a pawn break on the queenside.

notes.text: Theory ends here; the position is equal and both sides have fighting chances.
notes.original: The top move engine-wise, trying to re-maneuver the knight to a much more useful square. From here the theory pretty much ends and now it's simply chess from this point on. Both sides have clear fighting chances and the position is considered to be equal.

notes.text: You simply recapture the pawn.
notes.original: White simply recaptures the pawn.

notes.text: Black develops the light-squared bishop on a very active diagonal toward your e4 pawn.
notes.original: Developing the light-squared bishop on a very active diagonal.

notes.text: Your d5 pawn chases the knight away from c6.
notes.original: Chasing the knight away.

notes.text: Black retreats the knight back to a5.
notes.original: Retreating the knight back to a5.

notes.text: You answer by challenging the center yourself with d4, hitting the e5 pawn.
notes.original: White in response will also challenge the center with the move d5.

notes.text: Your knight hits the e4 pawn; Black is active, but you are slightly better.
notes.original: White moves the knight in order to attack the e pawn which will usually be taken. As you can see, black has gained a lot of activity and this line resembles something very similar to the Marshall Attack however black has not sacrificed a pawn. Black aims to put the bishop on d6 and put pressure on the king-side and to get their knight back into the game. White will usually play Qb1 at some point in order to try and win the pawn. White is considered to be slightly better in this position.

notes.text: d4 is your only really good move; it hits e5 now that Black's knight has left c6.
notes.original: White's only really good move is d4. Any other move would be too slow and be considered as inferior because it's not taking advantage of the fact that the knight has just moved from c6. The move d4 also allows the knight too re-maneuver itself towards the king-side which is very thematic of the Ruy Lopez.

notes.text: Black's knight reaches d7; now Black wants c5, Re8, Bf8 and Bb7, and both sides finish their plans.
notes.original: Black continues with their own plan which was to get the knight to d7. Now black can try and push for c5, get the rook on e8, get the dark-squared bishop to f8, the light-squared bishop can go to b7, and so on. In this variation, both sides can complete their plans which little fighting.

notes.text: Your setup is ideal: both knights are well placed and your bishops stare at the kingside.
notes.original: White has now achieved his perfect opening setup. Both knights are perfectly placed for attacks, the bishops are staring at the king-side, and the queen is ready to jump into h5.

notes.text: The g6 move also opens the diagonal for Black's bishop on f8.
notes.original: This is a must-play move for black because black has to prevent Nf5. Black has now opened up the diagonal for his f8 bishop.

notes.text: Black must play g6, or your knight jumps to f5.
notes.original: This is a must-play move for black because black has to prevent Nf5. Black has now opened up the diagonal for his f8 bishop.

notes.text: Your kingside development is finished; now you try to gain an edge there by exchanging rooks.

notes.original: The bishops here may get exchanged here and this resembles some closed Ruy Lopez lines. As you can see, this doesn't resemeble anything similar to the Marshall Attack.

notes.original: This is not a very common move but it holds a very simple concept. The idea is to simply try to open up the file for white's rook. notes.text: You simply develop another piece with this knight move.
notes.original: White continues normally and develops.

notes.text: Black finally castles and gets the king out of the center.
notes.original: Black will finally get their king out of the center.

notes.text: Your a-pawn attacks the b5 pawn, and you want to trade rooks.
notes.original: White wants to attack the b-pawn and exchange rooks.

notes.original: White stick to their main plan and takes the b-pawn anyway, opening up the file for their rook.

notes.original: Black recaptures the rook and now in this position, white is considered to be slight better but it's a fairly even position. Most of the top games from this point have ended in a draw.

notes.text: Retaking with the queen is not advised; you are better here than after the bishop retake.
notes.original: This is not advised, white is considered better in this position than if black had taken with the bishop.

notes.text: You challenge the center at once, hitting the e5 pawn, since d5 isn't yet possible for Black.
notes.original: White is challenging the pawn in the center immediately and is trying to take advantage of the fact that d5 can't be played straight away. Black's knight would be pinned to the king

notes.original: The point of this move is simply to attack the bishop and to allow black to play d5.

notes.original: White moves the bishop away which is the only sensical move for white.

notes.text: Black wants a well-centralized structure, not the pawn; now you can strike back and retake on e5.
notes.original: The idea for black was not to win the pawn, but to have a well-centralized structure. This is white's chance to strike back in the center and white will take back the pawn.

notes.text: You finally win the pawn back on e5.
notes.original: White finally recaptures the pawn and is reinforced by the knight on f6.

notes.text: Black develops and fixes a strategic problem by reinforcing the d5 weakness.
notes.original: Black here is not only developing but also solving their strategic problems. In this case, they're reinforcing the weakness on d5.

notes.text: This is the Bernstein Variation, your most common move: you want to get rid of the e4 knight.
notes.original: This is white's most common move and this is known as the Bernstein Variation. White simply wants to get rid of the knight on e4.

notes.text: An alternative: your bishop gets the safer, more active c2 diagonal, but this allows Black's Bc5.
notes.original: This is an alternative option that white can go for. The idea is simply to get the light-squared bishop onto c2, a much safer and more active diagonal for the bishop. The drawback to this move is that it allows black to play Bc5.

notes.text: Your bishop on e3 covers c5 and stops Black's dangerous attack with Bc5.
notes.original: This is another alternative option for white, preventing black's dangerous attack with Bc5.

notes.text: Black retreats the knight and seems to threaten your bishop, but taking it is not necessarily good.
notes.original: Black simply retreats the knight and seemingly threatens to take the light-squared bishop. However, taking the bishop is not necessarily that good.

notes.text: Black simply develops and prepares to castle.
notes.original: This is an alternative option for black, simply developing and preparing to castle their king.

notes.text: Your c3 pawn frees the c2 square, a much safer diagonal for your bishop.
notes.original: White can now play c3 and get the bishop on the c2 square, a much safer diagonal.

notes.original: Instead of trying to take the bishop on b3, black goes for simple development and tries to castle their king.

notes.original: Let's say black decides to take the bishop on b3 anyway.

notes.original: Black tries to get rid of the c3 pawn in order to get more central squares for their knight.

notes.original: White gets their bishop on c2. This is the most useful and the safest position for white's light-squared bishop which, once again, is one of white's most useful pieces in this opening,

notes.original: White re-positions the d-knight in order to add additional pressure onto the d4 pawn.

notes.original: Black simply pushes the pawn, now having a passed pawn in the center and attacking white's light-squared bishop.

notes.original: White moves the light-squared bishop to the only open square that's left, maintaining the pressure on black's d-pawn.

notes.text: Black takes your knight and threatens your rook; recapture with the pawn, since taking with the queen would be costly.
notes.original: Black captures white's knight, threatening to capture the rook as well. Black is also hoping that white captures with the queen but this would be a costly mistake.

notes.original: White simply recaptures the knight, opening up the a-file for their rook.

notes.original: White simply moves the rook up one square, attacking the over-extended pawn.

notes.original: White simply recaptures the bishop with the rook.

notes.original: White moves the knight to probably the most useful and safest square.

notes.text: Your bishop reaches c5 and threatens to capture the rook on f8.
notes.original: White sticks to their plan of getting the bishop to c5 and is threatening to capture the rook.

notes.text: Black ignores your threat and takes the knight, now threatening a discovered check and a dangerous attack.
notes.original: Black ignores this threat and takes the knight anyways, threatening a discovered check and a dangerous attack.

notes.text: Taking with the f-pawn is your only move.
notes.original: White's only move is to take with the f-pawn.

notes.text: Black's rook leaves danger. The position is roughly equal, but Black's kingside attack means you must play carefully.
notes.original: Black gets their rook out of danger. From this point, the position is pretty much dead even although black has a dangerous attack on the king-side. White should play very carefully from this point forward. The position branches out from here, feel free to study the top games from this position.

notes.text: Black continues by bringing the rook into the attack.
notes.original: Black continues by getting their rook into the attack.

notes.text: You probably want to reroute the knight to g3 again, and this opens your bishop's diagonal.
notes.original: White is possibly preparing to re-maneuver their knight to g3 once again. White also opens up the diagonal for their bishop.

notes.text: The engine calls this equal, but Black's position is very pleasant; White avoids it and most games are drawn.
notes.original: Black continues the attack with Ne5. The position is considered to be equal according to the engine but black is in a very favorable position and white has tried to avoid this line over time. Most games from this position have ended in a draw.

notes.text: Black simply develops and will castle to get the king out of the center.
notes.original: Black will simply develop and get their king out of the center.

notes.text: Black goes for the attack anyway, and the bishop hits your bishop on e3.
notes.original: Let's say black tries to go for the attack anyway.

notes.text: You prepare to bring your bishop to c2.
notes.original: White prepares to get their bishop on c2.

notes.text: Black castles, getting the king out of the center.
notes.original: Black gets their king out of the center.

notes.text: Your knight again tries to chase Black's knight away from e4.
notes.original: White once again is trying to expel the knight from e4.

notes.text: Black centralizes the queen and lines it up with the bishop; the position is about even.
notes.original: Black centralizes the queen, also creating a battery with the light-squared bishop. The position branches out in multiple ways, feel free to look at some top tier games to see how they ended. The position here is pretty much even.

notes.text: You happily trade bishops, because Black's dark squares become much more vulnerable.
notes.original: White is more than happy to exchange bishops in this position. The reason for this is because the dark-squared complex has now become much more vulnerable.

notes.text: Black must recapture the bishop; from here you have several options, mostly developing a knight.
notes.original: Black's only move is to recapture the bishop. From here the position branches, white has multiple options from this point. Most of them include developing one of white's knights. Feel free to look at how the top tier games went on from this position.

notes.text: Black defends the pawn with f6, the main line.
notes.original: Black defends the pawn with the move f6 which is considered to be the main line.

notes.text: Qd6 is another way for Black to defend the e5 pawn, besides f6.
notes.original: This is an alternative to f6.

notes.text: Bg4 is another option for Black instead of f6.
notes.original: This is an alternative to f6.

notes.text: After Nf6 you can take the e5 pawn, since Black cannot win it back safely.
notes.original: If black plays this move, now you can take the pawn because black can no longer win back the pawn without blundering.

notes.text: This is basically your only move here: you challenge the center at once.
notes.original: This is white's most common and basically the only move after f6 by far. White wants to challenge the center immediately

notes.text: Black's best option: taking the pawn removes your central threat.
notes.original: This is black's best option, attempting to dismiss white's central threat.

notes.text: Nxd4 is the main line; avoid trading queens if you can, though a trade would not hurt you.
notes.original: White could've taken with the queen, but the main line is Nxd4 and is in my opinion, the best move. At this point, black doesn't have to play c6 but it is the best move. If you're playing as white, if you can avoid trading queens, do so. However, trading pieces wouldn't be harmful to white because of your pawn majority once again.

notes.text: Black pushes c5 to attack your knight and force an early queen trade.
notes.original: Black should push c5 in order threaten white's knight and force an early queen trade.

notes.text: Your knight leaves the attack and opens the door to a queen trade.
notes.original: White's knight gets out of danger, meanwhile opening up the opportunity for a queen trade.

notes.text: Black trades queens early to reach a smoother endgame.
notes.original: Black exchanges queens early on to have a smoother endgame.

notes.text: You recapture with the rook to take control of the d-file.
notes.original: White recaptures the queen with the rook in order to take control of the d-file.

notes.text: Black's bishop eyes your rook on d1 and will take it unless you react.
notes.original: Black threatens to capture the rook on d1.

notes.text: A very common line: you still need to develop your queenside, and central control will matter.
notes.original: This is a very common line after the exchange variation. White still needs to develop its pieces on the queenside. The side that controls the most central squares from this point will probably win the game.

notes.text: Black moves the bishop out of danger onto an active diagonal.
notes.original: Black needs to get their bishop out of danger and get on active diagonal.

notes.text: Be3 develops your bishop and, with the knight, hits the c5 pawn.
notes.original: White wants to capture the hanging pawn on c5 so they play Be3. This move also develops the bishop from c1.

notes.text: Black reinforces the c5 pawn with b6, along with the dark-squared bishop.
notes.original: Black reinforces the c-pawn with b6 along with their dark-squared bishop.

notes.text: This is the Gligoric main line: you lead in development, but your a1 rook is stuck.
notes.original: This was the main line of the exchange variation. This is known as the Gligoric Variation. White has a clear lead in development however, white cannot effectively use his a-rook at the moment which could be seen as a slight disadvantage. Despite all of this, the position is considered to be equal and both sides have fighting chances. The possible ideas of this position are shown above, but feel free to experiment.

notes.text: You take the free pawn on e5 and gain control of the center.
notes.original: White takes the free pawn on e5, taking control of the center at the moment.

notes.text: Qd4 forks your knight and e4 pawn, but with your king safe, simply retreat the knight.
notes.original: Black can no longer play this move because white's king is no longer in the center. If black does however, simply retreat the knight.

notes.text: Your knight retreats with gain of time, hitting the queen and keeping the center.
notes.original: White retreats the knight, attacking the queen and maintaining the control in the center.

notes.text: If Black grabs the pawn, Re1 pins the queen to the king and wins it.
notes.original: If black still takes the pawn anyway, congratulations, black has just lost the game. Black's queen is now pinned to the king after white plays Re1 to win the queen.

notes.text: A good beginner trap: the queen is pinned to the king, so Black must take the rook.
notes.original: This is a very good trap for beginners. If black plays this line, once again, the queen is pinned to the king which means black has to take the rook.

notes.text: Your queen blocks the check and forces a queen trade, since Black's queen is pinned.
notes.original: White blocks the queen's check with queen, forcing a queen trade. Black must take back because black is also pinned to the king.

notes.text: Your only legal move is to take back the queen with the king.
notes.original: White's only legal move is to take back the queen.

notes.text: With castling rights gone you are worse; as White, never take the e4 pawn right away.
notes.original: After this point, black is simply better. Black will continue to develop and white is at a disadvantage due to the fact that they have forfeited castling rights. If you're playing as white, never take the pawn on e4 right away.

notes.text: Black's f-pawn backs up the e5 pawn to reinforce the center.
notes.original: Black wants to reinforce the center.

notes.text: You still challenge the e5 pawn with your d-pawn anyway.
notes.original: White still decides to challenge the e5 pawn anyway.

notes.text: Black simply takes the pawn, and it now hits your knight on c3.
notes.original: Black's best response is to just take the pawn, putting pressure on white's knight.

notes.text: You shouldn't trade queens just yet.
notes.original: White shouldn't trade queens just yet.

notes.text: Black wants the queen trade, so the c-pawn attacks your knight on d4.
notes.original: Black does want to trade queens however so black puts pressure on the d-knight.

notes.text: You had to retreat the knight, or Black would win material.
notes.original: White must retreat the knight or black will gain material.

notes.text: Black goes for an early queen trade, with check.
notes.original: Black goes for an early queen trade.

notes.text: Luckily you can retake the queen with the knight instead of the king.
notes.original: Fortunately for white, they don't have to take back the queen with the king and they do so with the knight.

notes.text: Black develops the light bishop and prepares to castle long.
notes.original: Black develops their light-squared bishop and prepares to castle long.

notes.text: Your bishop develops and puts pressure on the c7 pawn.
notes.original: White develops their dark-squared bishop, putting pressure on the c7 pawn.

notes.text: Black castles long so the rook takes the d-file, hitting your knight on d1.
notes.original: Black castles long, allowing their rook to take control of the d-file and protecting the pawn on c7 as well.

notes.text: Your knight steps out of the pressure coming from Black's rook.
notes.original: White moves their knight out of the pressure coming from black's rook.

notes.text: Black simply develops the knight.
notes.original: Black simply develops their knight.

notes.text: Your rook challenges the rook on d8 so Black doesn't keep control of the d-file.
notes.original: White wants to challenge the rook on d8 so that their rook doesn't maintain control over the d-file.

notes.text: Black takes the rook rather than let you take control of the file.
notes.original: Black should take the rook and not allow them to take control of the file themselves.

notes.text: You have to retake with the king here, for a long-term reason shown later.
notes.original: White has to take with the king here. There's a long-term reason for this and I'll show you why.

notes.text: Taking the rook with the knight is a mistake: it gives away the a2 pawn.
notes.original: Let's say white had captured with the knight. This is a mistake because now white has just given away a pawn.

notes.text: Black gains kingside space and kicks your dark-squared bishop with the g-pawn.
notes.original: Black is trying to gain space on the king-side and is expelling the dark-squared bishop.

notes.text: The a2 pawn looks free, but you can trap the bishop with b3.
notes.original: Black may think that this is a free pawn because it's undefended, but this is not the case. White can simply trap the bishop with the move, b3.

notes.text: You simply get your bishop out of danger.
notes.original: White is simply getting their bishop of danger.

notes.text: Black is a bit more active because you never castled; castling was better, but this is still playable.
notes.original: Black has a bit more aggressive position because white didn't castle in the beginning and in my opinion, castling is much better option than playng this line, but it's still playable as white.

notes.text: Now Black's bishop is trapped and can be won later.
notes.original: Now black's bishop is trapped and can be taken later.

notes.text: Black takes the pawn and weakens your queenside, with no fear of being trapped.
notes.original: Black can capture the pawn and weaken white's queen-side safely without the fear of getting trapped.

notes.text: If White still tries to trap the bishop, Black simply pushes the c-pawn.
notes.original: If white tries to do so anyway, just push your c-pawn.

notes.text: Black's pawn hits your b3 pawn, so you have to push it.
notes.original: White's pawn is now receiving too much pressure and has no choice but to push.

notes.text: You push the pawn rather than capture on c4.
notes.original: White doesn't want to capture in this position, so they push their pawn.

notes.text: Black's bishop is free again; taking c3 is fine, but your overextended pawns leave Black better.
notes.original: Black's bishop can now go free. White can capture the pawn with no problem, but the issue is that now white has two over-extended pawns black is simply better.

notes.text: Black's best reply is simply to take the pawn.
notes.original: Black's best option is simply to take the pawn.

notes.text: You take on d4 and offer a queen trade.
notes.original: White initiates a queen-trade by taking the pawn on on d4.

notes.text: Black should just accept the queen trade.
Retaking with the knight is your only sensible move, unless you want to play without a queen.
notes.original: This is simply white's only move unless they plan on playing without a queen for the rest of the game.

notes.text: Black develops the bishop and prepares to castle long.
notes.original: Black develops their bishop and prepares to castle long.

notes.text: You simply develop your dark-squared bishop.
notes.original: White simply develops their dark-squared bishop.

notes.text: Black castles long, getting ready to open the d-file for the rook.
notes.original: Black castles long and prepares to open up the d-file for their rook.

notes.text: You develop again and reinforce your e4 pawn.
notes.original: White is developing once again and reinforcing their pawn on e4.

notes.text: Black pins your knight to the king and indirectly pressures e4; the position is fairly equal.
notes.original: Black now pins the knight to the king, indirectly challenging the e4 pawn as well. This line is known as the Alekhine variation. Basically, white wanted to remove the queen early on so that in the endgame, white may have better chances considering their majority on the king-side. This is a fairly equal position and it can lead to interesting games.

notes.text: The main line: Nc3 develops, challenges the center, and prepares to bring your a-rook to the d-file.
notes.original: This considered to be the main line of the Berlin Wall Defense. The point of this move is to develop and challenge the center and for white to get its a-rook into the game and control the d-file.

notes.text: Your h3 shows your kingside pawn majority and the plan to advance those pawns.
notes.original: This is immediately signifying white's pawn majority and their planning to advance the kingside pawns in the future.

notes.text: Black has three replies here: Be7, Be6 or h5, with h5 the main one.
notes.original: Black can play 3 different moves here, Be7, Be6, or h5. h5 is considered to be the main move.

notes.text: Black's h5 slows down your kingside pawn advance.
notes.original: Black plays this move in order to slow white down on the kingside.

notes.text: Once more, the e5 pawn is a drawback for you.
notes.original: Once again, you can see the downside of the e5 pawn.

notes.text: Your bishop is less strong here because of your e5 pawn.
notes.original: This bishop is not as strong because of the e5 pawn.

notes.text: This starts the main line of the Berlin Endgame; most lines draw. Study Kramnik, Caruana and Carlsen.
notes.original: This is the starting position of the main line of the Berlin Endgame. Most of lines from this point lead to a draw. Vladmir Kramnik, Fabiano Caruana, & Magnus Carlsen are great players to study the Berlin Endgame from.

notes.text: Black swings the rook to h6 to join the game. Never capture on e6.
notes.original: This is a very common maneuver in the Berlin Defense and is the second reason why black played h5. This is an important move because black has given up castling rights and this is the best way for black to get its rook in the game. White should never capture on e6.

notes.text: Black's knight heads for g6, where it will be more useful than on f5.
notes.original: Black plans to put his knight on g6 so that it can be useful rather than staying on f5.

notes.text: Your h3 prepares to push your kingside pawns forward.
notes.original: Prepares for a kingside pawn advance.

notes.text: Your b3 leads to a fianchetto: the bishop goes to b2.
notes.original: Leads to a fianchetto.

notes.text: Your a-rook is badly placed here, and this line is rare nowadays.
notes.original: The downside for white in this position is that his A-rook his not in a favorable position. This variation is not that common anymore.

notes.text: Black develops the bishop before solidifying e5, since Bxc6 can sometimes threaten to win that pawn.
notes.original: Black plays this move before solidifying his e5 pawn because in some positions, white will threaten to win the e5 pawn by capturing the knight on c6.

notes.text: Your c3 prepares d4 and gives your bishop a retreat to c2.
notes.original: This move serves multiple purposes. It prepares to push for d4 in order to challenge the center and it also allow white's bishop to retreat to c2 after black plays a6 and b5.

notes.text: Here c3 pays off: your bishop retreats to c2.
notes.original: Shows the benefit of c3.
